planting.note: Direct sow fresh seed as soon as the soil can be worked in spring; Turga is a long-season Hungarian heirloom that tolerates heavier soils better than many parsnip types.

directions: Sow seed thinly and shallowly in deeply worked, stone-free soil, keeping the bed evenly moist through the slow, erratic germination and thinning seedlings to a few inches apart once established. Turga is a Hungarian heirloom valued for producing stout, smoothly tapered roots that size up reliably even in soils too heavy or shallow for some other parsnip types, with a dense, creamy-white interior and a rich, distinctly sweet flavor. Leave roots in the ground through the first hard frosts before digging, since the cold converts starches to sugar and gives Turga its full sweet, almost nutty character. Because parsnip seed loses viability quickly, always start with fresh seed for the season.

planting.note: Direct sow in early to midsummer so roots bulk up in cool fall weather; Helenor is a widely grown commercial standard prized for uniform shape and good storage.

directions: Direct sow into loose, fertile soil and thin seedlings to six to eight inches apart, giving the globes plenty of room to size up evenly. Helenor produces smooth, round roots with a purple-blushed shoulder above soil level fading to pale cream below, and dense, pale orange flesh with a fine texture and a mild, well-balanced flavor. Its coloring develops early and evenly, and mature roots hold their quality well in cool storage through winter. Leave roots in the ground into cooler fall weather before harvest, since a touch of cold noticeably sweetens the flavor.

common_name: Golden Detroit Beet (Non-Bleeding Yellow Heirloom Beet)

planting.note: Direct sow as soon as soil can be worked in spring, or in late summer for a fall crop; Golden Detroit's yellow-orange roots never bleed color the way red beets do.

directions: Sow the multigerm seed clusters about half an inch deep in loose, fertile soil in full sun, and thin seedlings to three or four inches apart once true leaves appear. Golden Detroit is a yellow-fleshed sport of the classic Detroit type, producing round, orange-skinned roots that cook down to a warm mustard-gold color instead of bleeding red, so it can be roasted, pickled, or shaved raw into salads without staining hands or other ingredients. The flavor is sweet and mild, generally considered gentler and less earthy than red beet varieties, and the tender tops are excellent cooked as greens. Harvest at two to three inches across for the best texture, and keep the soil evenly moist throughout to prevent tough, fibrous roots.

common_name: Purple Glazer Garlic (Glazed Purple Stripe Hardneck Heirloom)

planting.note: Plant individual cloves pointed end up in fall, several weeks before the ground freezes, in loose, fertile, well-drained soil; Purple Glazer is a Glazed Purple Stripe type that needs a real winter chill to size up well.

directions: Plant cloves pointed end up, about two inches deep, in loose, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Purple Glazer is a Glazed Purple Stripe heirloom out of the Republic of Georgia, prized for its striking bulb wrappers of deep violet-purple washed with a metallic gold or silver sheen, wrapping six to nine plump, easy-to-peel cloves with a rich, balanced flavor that starts sweet and finishes with a gentle, lingering warmth. Like other hardnecks it sends up a coiling scape in early summer that should be cut once curled to redirect energy into bulb growth, and the scapes are excellent chopped into pesto or stir-fries. It stores respectably for a hardneck and performs best in regions with a genuinely cold winter to break dormancy, making it best suited to northern and mountain gardens.

common_name: Jermor Shallot (French Banana Shallot, RHS AGM)

planting.note: Plant sets four to eight weeks before the last frost in spring, or in fall in mild-winter regions; Jermor is a French-bred banana-type shallot noted for its elongated shape and refined flavor.

directions: Plant individual sets about an inch deep and six to eight inches apart, with the tip just at or slightly above the soil surface, and keep the bed weeded and evenly watered through spring growth. Jermor is a French 'banana' or échalion-type shallot bred in Brittany, producing clusters of medium to large, elegantly elongated bulbs with glossy rose-copper skin and pale pink-tinged flesh prized for its refined, mild-sweet flavor. Reduce watering once the foliage begins to yellow and fall over, then lift the bulbs and cure them in a warm, dry, airy spot for two to three weeks before trimming and storing. Well-cured bulbs keep for several months in cool, dry storage.

common_name: Griselle Shallot (French Grey Shallot, True Shallot)

planting.note: Plant small bulbs four to eight weeks before the last frost in spring; Griselle, the true French grey shallot, is grown from bulb divisions rather than seed and does not store as long as red or Dutch yellow shallot types.

directions: Plant individual bulbs about an inch deep and four to six inches apart in loose, well-drained soil, and each will multiply into a cluster of several new bulbs by midsummer. Griselle is regarded by French cooks as the only true shallot, a distinct species from common onion-derived shallots, forming small, teardrop-shaped bulbs under a papery grey-brown skin around pinkish flesh with fine purple veining and an intensely complex, refined flavor prized raw in vinaigrettes and salads. Reduce watering once the tops yellow and topple over, then lift the cluster and cure it in a warm, airy, shaded spot for one to two weeks. Because Griselle does not keep as long as red or Dutch yellow shallots, plan to use the harvest within a few months or replant a portion of the smaller bulbs the following season.

planting.note: Direct sow earlier than most beets, several weeks before the last frost under cover or cloches; Boltardy's outstanding resistance to premature bolting is what allows the early start.

directions: Sow the multigerm seed clusters half an inch deep in loose, fertile soil, thinning seedlings to three or four inches apart once true leaves appear. Boltardy is a Dutch-bred Detroit-type beet that has become one of the most widely grown home garden beets in Britain because it resists bolting to seed when exposed to the cold snaps and temperature swings of an early spring sowing, letting gardeners start the crop weeks ahead of standard varieties. It produces smooth-skinned, deep burgundy, globe-shaped roots with minimal internal ringing and a sweet, tender flavor well suited to boiling, roasting, or pickling. Keep the soil consistently moist for even root development and pull roots at two to three inches across for the best texture.
